title: Architecture & Design
lede: The core skill of the whole plan: turning requirements into a structure. Everything here answers one of two questions — what should drive this design, and how should the pieces talk to each other. The phase ends in C4 diagrams and five ADRs for a system you actually run.
source: Notes from Udemy: Software Architecture & Design of Modern Large Scale Systems — Michael Pogrebinsky

concepts.lede: The user does not always know what they need — but they know the problem. Gathering requirements early is critical because the cost of change grows over time.

items: **Functional / feature requirements** — what the system does. They do **not** determine the architecture.
**Quality attributes (non-functional)** — scalability, availability, performance. These dictate the architecture.
**System constraints** — the boundaries the system must operate within.
**Technical** — must use a given framework; on-premise versus cloud
**Business** — limited budget, hard deadlines, third-party integrations
**Regulatory / legal** — HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2

blocks.call: Some constraints have room for negotiation and others do not. Use loosely-coupled architecture so that the ones that move later do not force a rewrite.

cards: You are in a design meeting. The PM lists features, the CTO asks what determines the architecture. Which requirement type?
Non-functional requirements — the quality attributes.
Your startup has a strict budget, must use AWS, and handles EU user data. Which three constraint types?
Business (budget), technical (AWS), regulatory (GDPR).
A PM wants to change a core feature after six months of development. Why is this costly?
The cost of change grows over time — late requirement changes cost more in time, money and reputation.

concepts.lede: Use cases describe a situation in which the system is used. User flows turn each one into a step-by-step sequence of events.

num: Identify all actors and users in the system
Capture and describe every possible use case or scenario
Create user flows — expand each use case into a flow of events, each event carrying an **action** and its **data**

blocks.p: A diagram of the interactions between actors and objects over time. The right tool when the question is *what talks to what, in what order*.

blocks.call: Every action in a user flow maps to an API call. Do the flows first and the endpoint list writes itself.

cards: You are designing a login system. Walk the three steps to capture requirements via use cases.
Identify actors (users, admins) → capture use cases (login, reset password) → create user flows with an action and data per event.
During API design a colleague says they are not sure which endpoints are needed. Which earlier artifact would have mapped that out?
User flows — each action maps to an API call.
Your team needs to visualize how a user and the database interact over time during checkout. Which UML diagram?
A sequence diagram.

concepts.lede: Systems get redesigned not because a feature was missing, but because the system is not fast enough, does not scale, is slow to develop, is hard to maintain, or is not secure enough.

blocks.call: No single architecture provides every quality attribute. Some contradict each other outright — the job is picking the right trade-off, not maximising all of them.

items: **Response time** = processing time + waiting time (latency)
**Throughput** = tasks or data per second
Measure with **percentile distributions and tail latency** (P99, P95) — never simple averages

num: **Vertical (scaling up)** — a bigger machine. Easy, but a finite ceiling and low fault tolerance.
**Horizontal (scaling out)** — more machines. Near-unlimited, but adds complexity and may require code changes.
**Team scalability** — productivity versus team size. Modularize or split services to counter coordination overhead.

blocks.p: Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime) = **MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)**, where MTBF is mean time between failures and MTTR is mean time to recovery.

rows: a normal SaaS without an availability clause
what enterprise contracts ask for — deploys included
an architecture most companies cannot afford

items: **Failure prevention** — run on multiple servers (active-active, active-passive)
**Time redundancy** — retry until success or give up
**Failure detection** — monitoring and health checks
**Recovery** — automated failover
**SLA** — the contract with the customer, with penalties
**SLO** — the internal target you hold yourself to
**SLI** — the indicator you actually measure

cards: Your API reports an average response time of 200ms but P99 is 2s. Why is the average misleading?
Averages hide tail latency — use percentile distributions (P99, P95) to see true performance under load.
Your monolith is struggling under load. What is the quick cheap fix versus the scalable long-term fix?
Vertical — a bigger machine, cheap but a finite ceiling. Horizontal — more machines, complex but near-unlimited.
A client demands 99.99% availability. What is the maximum yearly downtime?
About 52.6 minutes — four nines.
Your system has MTBF = 720h and MTTR = 4h. Calculate availability.
Your payment service runs on a single server and it crashes. Which fault tolerance tactic was missing?
Failure prevention — run on multiple servers, active-passive or active-active.
The ops team argues about whether they met the contract. Which term is the contract, the target, and the measurement?
SLA is the contract, SLO the target, SLI the measurement.
concepts.drill: Year One · The number in the contract

concepts.lede: Organizes a system into tiers, each running on its own infrastructure. Multi-tier (separate infrastructure) is routinely confused with multi-layer (internal separation inside one application).

blocks.cap: The classic three-tier split — and where it goes wrong

items: Versatile for web-based services
The application tier scales horizontally on its own
Maintenance is simpler because business logic is centralized
The application tier tends to become **monolithic** — performance suffers and development slows as the codebase grows
**Two-tier** — presentation and application merged
**Four-tier** — adds a tier for API management

cards: Your team says they split controllers from services so they are multi-tier. Why is that actually multi-layer?
Multi-layer is internal separation within one application; multi-tier means separate infrastructure per tier.
Your three-tier app's application tier has grown huge and deploys are slow. What is the known failure mode?
The application tier becomes monolithic, hurting performance and slowing development.
Which tier must never expose business logic?
The presentation tier — it only handles user interaction.

concepts.lede: Small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its own database.

items: Difficult troubleshooting
Feature additions that ripple across the codebase
Team coordination problems and merge conflicts
One broken component takes everything down
**Loose coupling** — small teams own services independently
**Easier development and troubleshooting** — smaller codebases
**Performance and scalability** — each service scales horizontally on its own
**Fault isolation** — a failure or compromise is contained in one service
**Do not rush it** — without discipline you get a distributed Big Ball of Mud
Apply the **single responsibility principle** per service
Each service owns a **separate database**, or you have coupled them again through the data

blocks.call: Start monolithic — a modular monolith — and split when the complexity actually warrants it. Team scalability is the driver, not fashion.

cards: Your team of 30 is stuck: merge conflicts, slow deploys, one failing service takes the whole app down. What shift, and which two problems does it fix?
Microservices — independent teams and deployments, plus fault isolation.
An attacker compromises one microservice. Why does the whole app not fall?
Fault isolation — the issue is contained within that single service.
Two microservices share one database and every schema change breaks the other. Which best practice was violated?
Each service should own its separate database to avoid coupling.
A junior engineer proposes splitting a two-service app into twenty microservices on day one. What is the counter-argument?
Microservices add complexity — start monolithic and split when complexity warrants it, or you build a Big Ball of Mud.

concepts.lede: APIs are the contract between you and everyone who calls you. Once published, the contract is harder to change than the code behind it.

items: **Public** — open to any developer
**Private** — internal use inside the organization
**Partner** — specific partners, under an agreement
**Encapsulation** — clients must never need to understand your internals
**User-friendliness** — intuitive naming, consistent structure
**Idempotent operations** — repeated requests do not cause unintended outcomes
**Pagination** — large datasets are returned in bounded segments
**Asynchronous APIs** — long-running operations acknowledge immediately
**Versioning** — so changes ship without breaking consumers

blocks.p: RPC makes a remote call feel local, described by an Interface Description Language. A **server stub** listens, a **client stub** handles serialization, and DTOs are generated from the IDL.

items: Modern high-performance RPC from Google, 2015
**Transport** — HTTP/2
**IDL** — Protocol Buffers
Resource-oriented, resources identified by hierarchical URIs
**Stateless** — which is what makes it scale
**Cacheable** — clients store responses and reduce server load
POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes, GET retrieves

rows: HTTP/2 plus Protocol Buffers — fast and strongly typed
A client that needs one flexible query shape
flexibility moves to the client, and so does the cost

cards: Your startup builds a payment API. Banks get special terms, internal microservices use it, and any dev can try it. Which API type for each?
Partner (banks), private (internal), public (open developers).
A user clicks place order twice and gets charged twice. Which design practice was violated?
Idempotency — repeated requests should produce the same result.
Your API returns 10k records and times out. What pattern fixes this?
Pagination — return data in smaller segments.
Your backend service needs fast, typed, bidirectional calls to another service. REST or RPC?
RPC — specifically gRPC, with HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
Third-party developers need a public API to access your platform. REST or gRPC?
REST — resource-oriented, cacheable, stateless, widely adopted for public APIs.
What transport protocol and IDL does gRPC use?
HTTP/2 as transport, Protocol Buffers as the interface description language.
concepts.drill: Year One · The partner API, and Charged twice

concepts.lede: A single entry point that manages the complexity of a system with many services.

items: **API composition** — consolidates many APIs into one endpoint, so internal change does not reach consumers
**Centralized security** — authentication, authorization and rate limiting in one place
**Performance** — one client call instead of many, plus response caching
**Monitoring and alerting** — one place that sees all traffic
**Protocol translation** — bridges systems that speak differently
Never put **business logic** in the gateway — that rebuilds the monolith
It is a **single point of failure** — run multiple instances
Avoid optimizations that bypass the gateway and defeat the decoupling
**Open source** — Netflix Zuul
**Cloud** — AWS API Gateway, GCP API Gateway with Apigee, Azure API Management

cards: Your 15 microservices require every client to handle auth, rate limiting and service discovery. What solves this?
An API gateway — one entry point centralising auth, routing, rate limiting and monitoring.
A junior dev adds discount calculation logic to the API gateway. What is the problem?
Business logic in the gateway turns it into a monolith and a single point of failure.
concepts.drill: Build Bench · Cold start, and the trap in Black Friday

concepts.lede: Asynchronous communication that decouples the sender from the receiver — the single most useful move in this phase.

blocks.p: Synchronous communication requires both parties to be active at the same moment. That produces blocking waits for users, crashes under high traffic, and tight coupling between services. A broker lets the sender finish without waiting for the receiver.

items: **Message routing** — messages reach the right consumers
**Transformation** — convert between message formats
**Validation** — enforce message integrity
**Load balancing** — distribute work across consumers
**Pub/Sub** — the basis of event-driven architecture
Fault tolerance
High availability
Scalability
Trade-off: slightly added latency
**Open source** — Apache Kafka for high-throughput distributed event streaming, RabbitMQ for routed task messages
**Cloud** — AWS SQS, GCP Pub/Sub and Cloud Tasks, Azure Service Bus, Event Hubs and Event Grid

cards: Your order service calls payment and notification synchronously. During a flash sale, payments slow down and orders queue up. What pattern, and how does it help?
A message broker — it decouples sender from receiver so the order service does not block on slow dependencies.
A new analytics team wants to consume order events without modifying the order service. How?
Pub/Sub via a message broker — add a subscriber without changing the producer.
You need a high-throughput event stream for real-time analytics across 50 microservices. Kafka or RabbitMQ?
Apache Kafka — built for distributed event streaming at scale.

concepts.lede: Services communicate through events — immutable statements of change — instead of direct API calls.

items: **Event emitters (producers)** — publish events
**Event consumers** — react to them
**Event channel (message broker)** — routes between the two
**Decoupling** — a banking front-end emits user-action events while the account service consumes them, with no direct connection between them
**Easier integration** — mobile notifications or fraud detection subscribe without touching existing services
**Real-time processing** — immediate reaction to patterns in the stream
**Event sourcing** — store the events rather than the current state, and replay them to reconstruct any past state. Gives a solid audit trail and simpler error handling.
**CQRS** — separate read and write paths so each can be optimized independently

blocks.call: Events are immutable statements of change: facts that already happened. They are never overwritten or mutated the way state is.

cards: What are the three components of event-driven architecture?
Producers (emitters), consumers, and an event channel (message broker).
A banking app needs fraud detection and push notifications without modifying the account service. Which architecture?
Event-driven — new consumers subscribe to existing event streams.
Why are events called immutable statements of change?
They represent facts that already happened — never overwritten or mutated like state.
You need a full audit trail and the ability to reconstruct past states. Which pattern stores events instead of current state?
Event sourcing — replay stored events to rebuild state.

concepts.lede: Continuous processing of an infinite stream of events in real time — for anomaly detection, fraud detection and live metrics, where a delayed answer is a useless answer.

items: **Event time** — when it actually occurred, recorded in the payload
**Application / arrival time** — when it reached the consumer
**Processing time** — when the system processed it

blocks.p: In distributed systems events arrive late and out of order, which is exactly why these three diverge and why the distinction matters.
An infinite stream cannot be analysed whole, so it is cut into finite windows.

rows: Fixed, non-overlapping intervals; each event lands in exactly one window
Simple and cheap, but results only arrive at the end of each interval
A window duration plus an **advance interval**; windows overlap, so one event can appear in several
Frequent near real-time results, at the cost of memory, CPU and network

blocks.cap: A one-hour window advancing every minute produces a fresh answer every minute

blocks.p: A series of events reveals what one event cannot. One card transaction is unremarkable; two transactions in different countries minutes apart is a pattern.

blocks.call: Set the advance interval larger than the window and the windows stop overlapping and start skipping — effectively sampling. Useful for high-volume, low-variability streams.

cards: A fraud event happened at 12:00:00, reached your consumer at 12:00:09 and was processed at 12:00:11. Name the three timestamps.
Event time, application/arrival time, processing time.
Why can't you just use processing time for stream analytics?
Events arrive late and out of order — processing time attributes an event to the wrong period.
You need the hourly error rate refreshed every minute. Which windowing strategy, with what parameters?
A hopping window — one-hour duration with a one-minute advance interval.
You want each event counted exactly once in simple fixed buckets. Which strategy?
Tumbling windows — fixed, non-overlapping intervals.
Your hopping windows are eating memory and CPU. Why?
Overlapping windows must all be maintained at once, and each produces results.
One card transaction looks fine on its own, but the account is being defrauded. What does stream processing add?
Aggregation across a window — patterns across several events that no single event reveals.
concepts.drill: Build Bench · Black Friday, the analytics consumer

concepts.lede: Two answers to one tension: complete and accurate over all history, versus an answer about three seconds ago. Lambda runs a batch and a speed pipeline and merges them at read time; Kappa argues a retained log makes the batch half unnecessary.

rows: A bounded dataset at rest (HDFS, S3)
An unbounded stream off a broker
Accurate, complete, **replayable** — fix the logic and rerun
Millisecond latency; you react while the event matters
A terabyte scan takes hours; your view is always one window stale
Approximation — sketches, out-of-order arrivals, no un-processing

blocks.p: Fan the same raw stream down two independent pipelines. The **batch layer** is the source of truth; the **speed layer** is a stopgap covering only the gap since the last batch run. A **serving layer** answers each query by merging the two, then discards the real-time view once batch catches up.

blocks.call: The speed layer is allowed to be approximate because its errors are transient — every real-time view is eventually overwritten by a correct batch view.

num: **Duplicate business logic** — attribution, sessionization and fraud rules implemented twice, in two frameworks. Every change is a two-sided change.
**Divergence bugs** — batch says 4.1% CTR, stream says 4.4%, and you debug across two stacks to find which is lying.
**Operational weight** — two clusters, two pipelines, two monitoring setups, plus a serving layer that must merge correctly.

blocks.p: Kreps' reaction: drop the batch layer, keep **the log itself** as the immutable master dataset with long retention, and recompute by replaying it through a new version of the streaming job. One codebase. Event-time semantics, watermarks and exactly-once state made this viable in a way it was not in 2011.

Start streaming-first and add a batch path only for a concrete reason: regulatory reconciliation, backfills older than your log retention, or genuinely different algorithms for historical versus live computation.

cards: Your nightly job produced a wrong number because the logic had a bug. Why is this recoverable in batch but painful in streaming?
Batch keeps the immutable master dataset — fix the code and rerun. A stream processed each event once in flight, so there is nothing to recompute from unless the log itself is retained.
Lambda's speed layer uses approximations. Why is that acceptable?
Its errors are transient — every real-time view is eventually overwritten by a correct batch view covering the same window.
Which Lambda layer is the source of truth, and which is the stopgap?
The batch layer is the source of truth; the speed layer only covers the gap since the last batch run.
Your batch and speed layers report different conversion numbers for the same hour. What kind of bug is this?
A divergence bug — the structural consequence of implementing the same business logic twice in two frameworks. It is Lambda's main cost, not a one-off mistake.
You need to recompute a metric after a logic fix and you have no batch layer. How does Kappa handle it?
Replay the retained log from the beginning through the new version of the streaming job — the log *is* the master dataset.
You are designing a new analytics pipeline today. Lambda or Kappa, and what would change your mind?
Start with Kappa — one codebase, one framework. Add a batch layer only for regulatory reconciliation, backfills older than log retention, or genuinely different historical-vs-live algorithms.

concepts.lede: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the operations that modify data from the operations that read it.

blocks.p: When one database serves heavy reads and heavy writes, contention slows every transaction. CQRS gives reads and writes their own services and stores, each tuned for its workload.
The read side now lags the write side. Pairing CQRS with event sourcing handles this: changes publish events, consumers update the read model — **eventual consistency** at high performance.
A ranking service needs votes and comments. Rather than calling both services directly, it subscribes to their events — less load, better performance, no coupling.

blocks.call: CQRS is a real answer to a real problem, and it costs far more than it looks like it will. Reach for it when contention or aggregation actually hurts, not by default.

cards: Your single DB contends under mixed heavy reads and writes and transactions slow down. Which pattern, and how does it help?
CQRS — separate read and write paths into dedicated services and databases, each optimized for its workload.
After splitting reads and writes, a user's new post is not visible yet on the read side. What is this, and how is it resolved?
Eventual consistency — pair CQRS with event sourcing so consumers update the read state from events.
A ranking service needs votes and comments data without hammering those services. How?
Subscribe to their events instead of making direct service calls.

resources.w: Richards & Ford. The single best trade-off-thinking book in print, and the spine of this phase. ~20 hrs.

resources.t: Pogrebinsky's course *or* System Design Interview Vol. 1
resources.w: Same ground, two formats — the Udemy course if you learn by watching, Alex Xu if you learn by reading. Doing both is waste. Skip Vol. 2 unless you are interviewing.
Khononov is more thorough; Vernon's *Distilled* is a third the length for 80% of the strategic value. Read the strategic half only — tactical patterns can wait.
Martin is largely subsumed by Richards & Ford and more dogmatic about dependency direction than the trade-off framing you want. The second Pogrebinsky course heavily overlaps the first.
Context, container and one component diagram, plus five decision records — for your real system, not a hypothetical. Written *before* the code. This is capstone week 3–8.
